title: Be Memorable
tagline: The person they talk about back home.
description: Names, short stories, inside jokes, great goodbyes and the message the next morning. The small habits that make people remember you long after the trip.

vibe.setting: Rooftop, end of a great evening
vibe.scenario: You want to stay in touch with the travellers you've spent the evening with.

options.text: So… maybe we see each other again sometime, maybe, if the universe wants it?
Do you have WhatsApp? Or Instagram, or Facebook, or Viber? Or email? Which one do you use most?
Let's not lose this. What's your Instagram? I'll send the photo where we all look terrible.

vibe.why: A specific, funny reason makes sharing contacts feel natural, not like a request.

vibe.scenario: You've met Tom three times, but you've forgotten his name. He smiles: "Hey, Ram!"

options.text: Hey… buddy! My friend! How are you, man? So good to see you again! How's everything going with you?
Hey! Okay, confession: your face is saved in my brain, but your name fell out. One more time?
Hey, uh, Tim? Tony? Something with a T?

vibe.why: Admitting it with a smile is charming and fixes the problem forever. Guessing wrong hurts more than asking.

vibe.scenario: Someone asks, "What's the craziest thing that's ever happened to you?"

options.text: A cow once walked into my cafe, looked at the menu, and left. Honestly, fair review.
Hmm, nothing really crazy.
Okay, so, it was 2019, no, 2018, and I was with my cousin, no, my friend, and we were going to…

vibe.why: Short stories win. A setup, a surprise, and a punchline — in three sentences. Keep a few real ones ready.

vibe.scenario: A traveller mentions that tomorrow is their birthday.

options.text: Oh. How old will you be? Old!
Happy birthday for tomorrow! I hope you have a really nice day and a good time, wherever you go.
Then tomorrow the first tea is on me, and I'm making the whole cafe sing. Badly.

vibe.why: A tiny gesture on someone's birthday far from home is the kind of thing people remember for years.

vibe.scenario: A traveller you're chatting with has slipped off the same wobbly bench twice. They're laughing.

options.text: You're so clumsy.
Twice! The bench has chosen you. From now on, it's your bench.
Be careful!

vibe.why: An inside joke is a tiny shared story. Next time you meet, "your bench" is an instant laugh.

vibe.scenario: You see the traveller who told you yesterday about a monkey stealing their sunglasses.

options.text: Hi again! How are you? What have you been doing today? Did you go anywhere nice?
(Pretend you don't see them.)
The monkey survivor! Did you get new sunglasses, or are you still in hiding?

vibe.why: Remembering someone's story makes them feel seen. It's the fastest way to go from stranger to friend.

vibe.scenario: A traveller asks what to do on their last night in Pokhara.

options.text: Sunset on the lake, then the tiny momo place with no sign. Tell them I sent you and see what happens.
There are many good restaurants.
Just go anywhere. It's all the same, honestly, the food is the same everywhere on Lakeside.

vibe.why: A specific plan with a little mystery turns their last night into a story with you in it.

vibe.scenario: You're telling a long story and notice the traveller glancing at their phone.

options.text: Wait, wait, it gets better, there's so much more, just listen, so then the goat…
(Continue at the same pace.)
…long story short: I lost, the goat won. Anyway — do you have any animal enemies?

vibe.why: Cut to the punchline and hand them the stage. Knowing when to stop is part of being good company.

vibe.scenario: A traveller mentions they've been to thirty countries. You've never left Nepal.

options.text: Travelling is overrated. Nepal has everything, you don't need other countries.
Thirty! I'm on zero, so you're officially my window. Which one would you send me to first?
That's a lot of countries. I've never been out of Nepal, but maybe one day, if I can get a visa.

vibe.why: Honest about yourself, generous about them. Curiosity is more memorable than competition.

vibe.scenario: A traveller you've become friends with is leaving Pokhara for good.

options.text: Promise you'll come back? Promise? You have to promise. Say it!
Go on, go. And when someone asks about Nepal, tell them about the guy with the terrible jokes.
Bye, have a safe trip.

vibe.why: A light goodbye with a joke about yourself leaves a warm last picture. That's what they'll remember.

vibe.scenario: Last night a traveller bet you they could eat twenty momos. You want to follow up.

options.text: Hi. Hi. Hello? Why no reply? Did you see my message?
Morning! Did you survive the momo challenge, or should I call a doctor?
Hi, how are you? Hope you are well. How was your night? Did you sleep well?

vibe.why: A message that points to a shared moment feels personal and gives them something fun to reply to.

vibe.scenario: You both have great travel stories. The traveller starts telling theirs.

options.text: That reminds me of MY story, which is much crazier, so listen to this…
Nice story.
(Let them finish. Ask one good question about it. Tell yours later, if they ask.)

vibe.why: People remember how you made them feel. Letting them shine is more memorable than any story you tell.

cards.text: Then let's make sure. One last photo, and you promise to send me your first photo from home.
cards.why: Turns a feeling into a small ritual and a reason to stay in touch.

yesAnd.pattern: Turn a feeling into a ritual

cards.text: Ram — like the animal, but less hairy. And you're…?
cards.why: A tiny joke makes your name stick. Use your own name and your own hook.
Correct, and easy to forget again.

cards.text: Wait until you hear my serious side. It's even funnier.
cards.why: Accepts the compliment with another joke.
Arguing with a compliment makes the giver feel wrong.
Sounds like you don't believe them.

cards.text: Deal — it's going on the cafe wall so everyone knows I have international fans.
cards.why: Makes their promise feel special and fun.

yesAnd.prompt: Can I buy you a drink to say thank you?

cards.text: Only if you tell me the full story of that bus driver while we drink it.
cards.why: Accepts graciously and asks for a story in return.
Refusing a thank-you can feel like rejecting them.

yesAnd.prompt: We should definitely keep in touch.

cards.why: Sounds like it will never happen.

cards.text: Yes — give me your number and I'll send you the best sunset photo from today. Promise.
cards.why: Makes it real right now, with a specific reason.

yesAnd.prompt: I've told all my friends about you!

cards.text: Only good things, I hope. Did the monkey story make it in?
cards.why: Playful, and it brings back a shared memory.
Surprised, but no warmth to reply to.

yesAnd.prompt: This was the best day of my whole trip.

cards.text: Then we have to give it a name. What do we call today?
cards.why: A naming game makes the day an inside joke you share.
Polite, but it lets the moment pass.

upgrader.clunky: Okay, bye, nice to meet, okay, bye bye.
upgrader.why: A goodbye that says what the meeting meant to you is one they'll remember.

upgrader.clunky: Can I, um, have your number, maybe, if you want to give?
upgrader.why: State the goal ("let's stay in touch"), then ask. Confident and easy to answer.

upgrader.clunky: It was a very funny, very crazy story, the story about the goat.
tiles: and I still don't know why.
answers: and I still don't know why.
upgrader.why: Don't tell people a story is funny. Tell it short, and let them laugh.

upgrader.clunky: Sorry, I forgot your name, sorry, very bad memory, sorry.
tiles: I want to get it right.
answers: I want to get it right.
upgrader.why: "I want to get it right" turns forgetting into a compliment.

upgrader.clunky: When you come back to Nepal maybe you can tell me, message me, maybe.
upgrader.why: A specific promise is more memorable than "message me".

upgrader.clunky: My story is not so interesting but, um, okay, I will tell.
upgrader.why: Never apologise before a story. A teaser makes people want to hear it.

upgrader.clunky: Thank you for, like, everything, you are very very nice person.
upgrader.why: Thank people for something specific. It shows you noticed what they did.

upgrader.clunky: I think, maybe, we can meet again tomorrow, maybe same place?
upgrader.why: Short and confident. It sounds like a plan, not a hope.

dropIn.fact: The line "people will never forget how you made them feel" is often credited to Maya Angelou, though an earlier version is credited to Carl W. Buehner.
dropIn.source: Quote Investigator, "They May Forget What You Said, But They Will Never Forget How You Made Them Feel" (2014)
dropIn.prompt: Before a group dinner, a nervous friend asks, "What if I say something stupid?"

options.text: Then don't say anything.
There's a famous line, usually credited to Maya Angelou: people forget what you said, but never how you made them feel. So just make them feel good.
options.why: Takes the pressure off words and puts it on warmth.

options.text: Maya Angelou said people forget what you say but remember how you made them feel.
options.why: Close, but it doesn't turn into advice.

dropIn.fact: The serial position effect: people tend to remember the first and last items in a list better than the middle ones.
dropIn.source: Murdock, "The serial position effect of free recall", Journal of Experimental Psychology (1962)
dropIn.prompt: A friend asks, "Why do you always end conversations with a joke?"

options.text: Memory science — people remember the start and the end best. So I open warm and leave on a laugh.
options.why: Explains your habit with a fact, simply.

options.text: No reason.
options.why: There's a good reason, and it's interesting.

options.text: It's called the serial position effect. It means the first and last items in a list are remembered better than the ones in the middle.
options.why: Correct, but it's a lecture, and you never connected it to your habit.

dropIn.pattern: Explain a habit with a fact

dropIn.fact: In memory experiments, people remembered funny sentences better than serious versions of the same idea.
dropIn.source: Schmidt, "Effects of humor on sentence memory", Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition (1994)
dropIn.prompt: A traveller asks why you teach them Nepali words with silly jokes.

options.text: Jokes aren't serious, but they help.
Because funny sticks — there's research showing people remember humorous sentences better. So "mitho" comes with a dancing cook.
Sorry, I'll stop joking and be serious.

options.text: normal
unforgettable
options.why: Strong, warm and easy to understand.

options.text: pleasant

wordPower.meaning: So good you'll always remember it.
wordPower.example: The sunrise at Poon Hill was unforgettable.

wordPower.sentence: You are a very good storyteller.

options.text: natural
options.why: Says it comes easily to them — a lovely compliment.

options.text: consummate
fine

wordPower.meaning: (Before a noun) someone who is good at something without trying.

wordPower.sentence: I will remember this day for a long time.

options.text: commit this day to memory
options.why: Sounds like studying for an exam.

options.text: forget this day

wordPower.example: I'll never forget the day we got lost in Ghandruk.

wordPower.sentence: Your message this morning made me very happy.

options.text: made my day
options.why: A warm, very common phrase everyone knows.

options.text: gladdened me
confused me

wordPower.meaning: Made me very happy for the whole day.

wordPower.sentence: My grandfather is a very special person.

options.text: idiosyncratic
options.why: Means strange in a personal way, and few people know it.

options.text: singularly exceptional
options.why: Sounds like a speech, not a chat.

options.text: one of a kind
options.why: Warm and vivid: nobody else is like him.

wordPower.sentence: Our goodbye at the bus park was very sad.

options.text: quick
melancholic
bittersweet
options.why: Sad and happy together — exactly what a good goodbye feels like.

wordPower.meaning: Happy and sad at the same time.
wordPower.example: The last night of a great trip is always bittersweet.
